# Modbus Receiver

This receiver polls coils, discrete inputs, holding registers and input registers from Modbus TCP devices, such as PLCs, sensors and meters, and reports their values as metrics.

The receiver connects to a single Modbus TCP device or gateway, reads a
configured list of registers on every collection interval, and emits each value
as a gauge. The receiver is read-only: it only uses the Modbus read function
codes and never writes coils or registers.

## Supported devices

Any device or gateway that speaks **Modbus TCP** and supports the standard read
function codes:

| Register type | Function code | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `coil` | FC01 Read Coils | single bit |
| `discrete_input` | FC02 Read Discrete Inputs | single bit, read-only |
| `holding_register` | FC03 Read Holding Registers | 16-bit registers |
| `input_register` | FC04 Read Input Registers | 16-bit registers, read-only |

Not supported at this stage:

- **Modbus RTU and ASCII** (serial). Serial devices can be reached through a
  Modbus TCP gateway.
- **Modbus/TCP Security** (TLS). Connections are unencrypted and
  unauthenticated, as is typical for Modbus TCP.

### Data types

Values in holding and input registers are decoded according to `data_type`.
The number of registers read is derived from it:

| `data_type` | Registers | Reported as |
|---|---|---|
| `int16`, `int32`, `int64` | 1, 2, 4 | double gauge |
| `uint16`, `uint32`, `uint64` | 1, 2, 4 | double gauge |
| `float32`, `float64` (IEEE 754) | 2, 4 | double gauge |
| `bool` | - | coils and discrete inputs only, `0` or `1` |

`int64` and `uint64` values beyond 2^53 lose precision because they are reported as doubles.

### Byte orders

Modbus has no standard byte order for values that span several registers.
`byte_order` describes how the device lays out the bytes, where `ABCD` means
the most significant byte comes first:

| `byte_order` | Layout |
|---|---|
| `ABCD` | Big-endian (Modbus default, most PLCs) |
| `DCBA` | Little-endian, all bytes reversed |
| `BADC` | Big-endian words, bytes swapped within each word |
| `CDAB` | Word-swapped: low word first, big-endian bytes within each word |

If decoded values look wrong, for example huge or negative numbers, the byte
order is the most likely cause; check the device manual.

## Prerequisites

- The collector must be able to reach the device on TCP port `502` (or the port
  the device uses).
- Register `address` values are **0-based protocol addresses**, as sent on the
  wire. Many device manuals use 1-based reference numbers instead, such as
  `40001` for the first holding register or `30001` for the first input
  register; those correspond to `address: 0`.
- Each receiver instance holds one TCP connection to the device. Some devices
  and gateways allow only a few concurrent Modbus TCP connections, so account
  for other HMIs, SCADA systems or historians connected to the same device.

## Configuration

The following settings are required:

- `registers` (no default): List of registers to read on every poll. Must
  contain at least one entry. Each entry has:
  - `address` (required): 0-based register address.
  - `type` (required): `coil`, `discrete_input`, `holding_register` or
    `input_register`.
  - `data_type` (default = `bool` for coils and discrete inputs, `uint16` for
    registers): How to decode the value. See [Data types](#data-types).
  - `byte_order` (default = `ABCD`): Byte order of multi-register values. See
    [Byte orders](#byte-orders). Ignored for coils and discrete inputs.
  - `name` (no default): Optional label, emitted as the `modbus.name`
    attribute.

The following settings are optional:

- `endpoint` (default = `localhost:502`): Modbus TCP address of the device or
  gateway, as `host:port`.
- `unit_id` (default = `1`): Modbus unit (slave) ID, between `1` and `247`.
  Selects the device behind a gateway; most directly connected devices use `1`.
- `collection_interval` (default = `10s`): How often all registers are read.
  This value must be a string readable by Golang's
  [time.ParseDuration](https://pkg.go.dev/time#ParseDuration).
- `initial_delay` (default = `1s`): How long to wait before the first read.
- `timeout` (default = `0s`, no deadline): Deadline for one whole scrape of all
  registers. Registers not read when it expires count as failed. A request
  already in flight still runs until it completes or hits `request_timeout`.
- `request_timeout` (default = `5s`): Timeout for connecting and for each Modbus
  request.
- `reconnect_on_failure`: Backoff between reconnects to a device that is down,
  so a struggling PLC isn't redialed on every poll. It uses the standard
  collector
  [retry settings](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/tree/main/config/configretry):
  - `enabled` (default = `true`): When `false`, the receiver redials on every
    poll.
  - `initial_interval` (default = `10s`): Wait after the first failed connect.
  - `multiplier` (default = `1.5`) and `randomization_factor` (default = `0.5`):
    How the wait grows after each failure, and how much it is randomized.
  - `max_interval` (default = `60s`): Longest wait between reconnects.
  - `max_elapsed_time` (default = `5m`): Once a device has been down this long,
    every wait is `max_interval`. Reconnects never stop.

`collection_interval`, `initial_delay` and `timeout` are the standard
[scraper controller settings](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/tree/main/scraper/scraperhelper)
shared by other scraping receivers. `polling_interval` has been replaced by
`collection_interval`, and the per-request timeout that used to be `timeout` is
now `request_timeout`.

Example:

```yaml
receivers:
  modbus:
    endpoint: "192.168.1.10:502"
    unit_id: 1
    collection_interval: 10s
    registers:
      - address: 0
        type: holding_register
        data_type: float32
        byte_order: ABCD
        name: temperature
      - address: 0
        type: coil
        name: pump_status
```

Example with one receiver per device, since each receiver instance polls a
single device and unit ID:

```yaml
receivers:
  modbus/line1:
    endpoint: "192.168.1.10:502"
    registers:
      - { address: 0, type: holding_register, data_type: float32, name: temperature }
  modbus/line2:
    endpoint: "192.168.1.11:502"
    registers:
      - { address: 0, type: holding_register, data_type: float32, name: temperature }

service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [modbus/line1, modbus/line2]
      exporters: [debug]
```

The full list of settings exposed for this receiver are documented in
[config.go](./config.go) with detailed sample configurations in
[testdata/config.yaml](./testdata/config.yaml). A complete, runnable collector
configuration is in [config.example.yaml](./config.example.yaml).

## Metrics

Details about the metrics produced by this receiver can be found in
[metadata.yaml](./metadata.yaml) with further documentation in
[documentation.md](./documentation.md).

In summary:

| Metric | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `modbus.register.value` | Gauge | Decoded value of a holding or input register. |
| `modbus.coil.value` | Gauge (int) | `0` or `1` from a coil or discrete input. |
| `modbus.device.up` | Gauge (int) | `1` if the device answered the last poll, otherwise `0`. |

The two value metrics carry `modbus.register_address`, `modbus.unit_id` and
`modbus.register_type` and `modbus.name` (an empty string when `name` is not
configured).
`modbus.register.value` also carries `modbus.data_type` and
`modbus.byte_order`.

Each value metric is emitted once per scrape, with one data point per
register. `modbus.device.up` has one data point per scrape, with the
`modbus.unit_id` attribute, so a device that stops answering shows up as `0`
that you can alert on. Any metric can be turned off with the standard mdatagen `metrics` setting:

```yaml
receivers:
  modbus:
    metrics:
      modbus.coil.value:
        enabled: false
```

Values are reported with unit `1` because the receiver does not know the
engineering unit of a register.

All attributes come from the static configuration, so the number of time
series equals the number of configured registers. Don't put dynamic values
such as timestamps or IDs in `name`.

## Behavior

- **Startup:** The receiver starts without connecting. It connects on the first
  poll, so an unreachable device does not block collector startup.
- **Device unreachable:** `modbus.device.up` is reported as `0`, no register
  values are emitted, and every register counts as failed (see Reporting
  failed registers). The receiver waits out the `reconnect_on_failure` backoff
  before it connects again. Polls inside the backoff window report `0` without
  contacting the device.
- **Several receivers on one device:** Polls to the same `endpoint` are
  serialized across the collector, so receivers sharing a device or gateway
  take turns instead of polling it at once.
- **Connection lost during a poll:** The connection is closed, the remaining
  registers are skipped for that poll, values already read are still
  emitted, and `modbus.device.up` is `0`. The receiver reconnects on the next
  poll.
- **Device busy (exception 06):** The device is overloaded, so the remaining
  registers are skipped for that poll and later polls wait out the
  `reconnect_on_failure` backoff. The connection stays open, and
  `modbus.device.up` stays `1`, since the device answered.
- **Modbus exception or invalid response for one register:** For example an
  illegal data address, or a response too short for the `data_type`. The
  register is skipped, the remaining registers are still read on the same
  connection, and `modbus.device.up` stays `1`.
- **Reporting failed registers:** When some registers fail, the values that
  were read are still emitted, and the failures are returned as one partial
  scrape error. The collector logs one error per scrape listing them, and
  counts them in `otelcol_scraper_errored_metric_points`.
- **Load on the device:** Each register is read with its own request, one at a
  time. Keep `collection_interval` conservative on production devices.

## Using this receiver in a collector

This receiver is not included in the OpenTelemetry Collector Contrib
distribution. Add it to your own distribution with the
[OpenTelemetry Collector Builder](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/custom-collector/)
(`ocb`):

```yaml
receivers:
  - gomod: github.com/otel-industrial/otel-industrial-resources/otel-industrial-collector/receiver/modbusreceiver v0.0.1 # use the latest released tag
```

This component is built and tested against collector v0.163.0. Use the same
`otelcol_version` in your builder manifest.

To build and run a local test collector, or try the receiver against the
included simulator without hardware, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md).
